question: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.

raiseTranscript.text: After our team pivoted from building internal tools to a customer-facing product, my backlog shifted from backend scripts to supporting the new onboarding flow. I asked my manager what success looked like in the new setup and spent two weeks pairing with the frontend lead to learn the stack.
What was the outcome on your work?

I delivered the first version of the onboarding emails two weeks early and got feedback that the copy reduced support tickets by about 15%. I still check in weekly on whether the priorities are still right.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Reorg/pivot moved candidate from internal tools to customer onboarding
Asked manager for success criteria, paired to learn new stack
Outcome: delivered early, 15% drop in tickets; continues to check priorities
Follow-up: How did you handle the uncertainty? - Focused on clarifying expectations and learning quickly
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Adaptability for a junior. Story shows the candidate treated the pivot as a scope change rather than a disruption, proactively clarified expectations with their manager, and used pairing to close a skill gap. Quote: "I still check in weekly on whether the priorities are still right." This demonstrates ownership of their own work and coachability. The result stayed local but was measurable. Biggest strength is turning ambiguity into a clear plan without needing hand-holding.

lowerTranscript.text: We got told the product direction changed and I had to drop my project. I finished what I could and waited for the new assignment.
How did you figure out what to work on next?
My manager eventually assigned me something else. It took a couple weeks to ramp.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Candidate dropped work and waited passively for new assignment
Took weeks to ramp after manager finally assigned new task
No evidence of clarifying expectations or seeking context
Follow-up: How did you handle the uncertainty? - Waited for manager to drive
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Adaptability for a junior. The candidate showed no initiative to understand the new direction or close their own knowledge gaps, instead waiting for the manager to assign work. Quote: "My manager eventually assigned me something else." This leaves the impression that change is something that happens to them rather than something they navigate. The gap is lack of ownership over their own learning and priorities during a shift.

raiseTranscript.text: When leadership decided to sunset our platform and move customers to the acquired product, my charter shifted from owning the old service to driving migration for three enterprise accounts. I mapped the gaps, ran weekly syncs with the other team, and created a shared runbook so support wouldn't get surprised.
One team kept deprioritizing the migration work. I escalated the risk with data on ticket volume and got the migration added to their OKRs.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Sunset decision moved candidate to lead migration for three accounts
Built cross-team runbook and ran syncs; escalated with data to protect support
Outcome: migration added to other team's OKRs
Follow-up: What resistance did you hit? - Used metrics to influence without authority
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Adaptability for a senior. Candidate took a structural change (sunset) and converted it into cross-team coordination work, using data to influence another team to reprioritize. Quote: "I escalated the risk with data on ticket volume." Shows influence without authority and some early signs of protecting downstream teams. Biggest strength is treating the strategy shift as an opportunity to create leverage rather than just absorbing the change.

lowerTranscript.text: Leadership moved us to a new product line. I updated my roadmap and kept shipping the features that were already approved.
Did the new direction require any coordination?
I mostly stayed in my lane and let the PMs figure out the overlaps.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Candidate updated personal roadmap but stayed within existing approved work
No cross-team coordination or influence on overlaps
Outcome: stayed in lane while PMs handled alignment
Follow-up: Did the new direction require any coordination? - Deferred entirely to PMs
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Adaptability for a senior. The candidate treated the strategy shift as a personal roadmap update rather than a signal to align broader teams. Quote: "I mostly stayed in my lane." This misses the expectation that seniors should surface and resolve cross-team friction created by the change. The gap is lack of influence without authority during a structural pivot.

raiseTranscript.text: After the reorg combined two teams under one VP, my group lost two headcount and had to absorb the support rotation. I ran a skills mapping exercise with the team, identified two people who wanted to grow into on-call, and redistributed the rest of the work so no one person's load increased more than 10%.
How did you handle the people who were unhappy?
I had 1:1s with the two most vocal engineers, shared the data on why the rotation was necessary, and offered to rotate them off after six months if they still wanted out.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Reorg reduced headcount and added support rotation to the team
Ran skills mapping, redistributed load, capped increase at 10%
Handled pushback with data and time-bound commitment in 1:1s
Follow-up: How did you handle the people who were unhappy? - Used transparency and offered an exit ramp
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Adaptability for a manager. Candidate absorbed a headcount cut and new operational load by redesigning team processes and addressing individual concerns directly. Quote: "I offered to rotate them off after six months if they still wanted out." Shows ability to create leverage through the team and handle underperformance risk before it appears. Biggest strength is turning a top-down change into a structured team adjustment with clear guardrails.

lowerTranscript.text: After the reorg I told the team we had to pick up the extra work and asked everyone to step up. A couple people left over the next quarter.
How did you decide who took on what?
I assigned the new rotation to the more junior folks since they had more availability.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Told team to absorb extra work without redesigning processes
Assigned rotation to junior members; two people left in following quarter
No evidence of skills mapping or addressing concerns proactively
Follow-up: How did you decide who took on what? - Loaded juniors without discussion
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Adaptability for a manager. The candidate passed the structural change directly to the team without redesigning ownership or load. Quote: "I assigned the new rotation to the more junior folks." This created attrition and shows no skill in creating leverage or developing people through change. The gap is treating the reorg as a simple delegation exercise rather than a team design problem.

raiseTranscript.text: When the board pushed for profitability in 18 months, we had to move from growth-at-all-costs to a focused set of three product lines. I restructured the org into two divisions, moved 40% of engineering under a new platform group, and created a sunset plan for the remaining products with clear customer communication.

Keeping the platform team from becoming a bottleneck while still delivering the three lines. We sequenced platform work behind the highest-revenue product first and published a quarterly capacity model so every GM could plan.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Board-mandated profitability pivot forced focus from many products to three lines
Restructured into two divisions, moved 40% of eng to platform, created sunset plan
Sequenced platform work behind top revenue product and published capacity model
Follow-up: What was the hardest trade-off? - Used quarterly capacity model to manage dependencies
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Adaptability for an exec. Candidate converted a board-level profitability mandate into an org redesign and product sunsetting process while protecting execution on the remaining lines. Quote: "We sequenced platform work behind the highest-revenue product first and published a quarterly capacity model." Demonstrates strategic judgment on trade-offs and long-term leverage through structure. Biggest strength is treating the shift as an opportunity to simplify the business rather than just cutting scope.

lowerTranscript.text: The board told us to focus, so we picked our top three products and told the other teams to wind down. Some products took longer than expected to shut off.
How did you handle the teams whose products were deprioritized?
We gave them six months to find new roles internally or exit.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time company strategy, structure, or direction shifted and your role or priorities changed as a result.
Selected three products and directed remaining teams to wind down
Gave six-month window for internal moves or exit
No evidence of sequencing, capacity planning, or protecting remaining execution
Follow-up: How did you handle the teams whose products were deprioritized? - Time-boxed exit without redesign
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Adaptability for an exec. The candidate executed the profitability mandate through blunt product selection and headcount process rather than org or operating model redesign. Quote: "We gave them six months to find new roles internally or exit." Misses the expectation that execs create sustainable leverage and manage long-term business impact. The gap is lack of strategic judgment on how to sequence and protect the focused bets.

diagnostic.signal: Ownership of change vs. waiting for direction
diagnostic.junior: Raises: clarifies expectations and learns new skills; Lowers: waits for manager assignment
diagnostic.senior: Raises: uses data to influence cross-team reprioritization; Lowers: stays in lane
diagnostic.manager: Raises: redesigns team load and addresses concerns in 1:1s; Lowers: assigns extra work without redesign
diagnostic.exec: Raises: sequences work and publishes capacity model; Lowers: time-boxes exits without operating model changes

diagnostic.junior: Raises: checks in on priorities after delivery; Lowers: no follow-up
diagnostic.senior: Raises: protects support with runbook; Lowers: ignores overlaps
diagnostic.manager: Raises: caps individual load increase at 10%; Lowers: creates attrition
diagnostic.exec: Raises: protects remaining product lines with sequencing; Lowers: leaves wind-down unmanaged

diagnostic.signal: Use of structure or process to absorb ambiguity
diagnostic.junior: Raises: pairs to close skill gap; Lowers: passive ramp
diagnostic.senior: Raises: creates shared runbook; Lowers: no coordination mechanism
diagnostic.manager: Raises: skills mapping + time-bound commitments; Lowers: direct delegation
diagnostic.exec: Raises: org restructure + quarterly capacity model; Lowers: product list only
